text: Book II of the Republic contains two arguments that later readers have often treated separately. The first builds a city from scratch, though Socrates presents the exercise less as political theory than as a way of seeing the soul at a larger scale: the city serves as a magnified image of the person (Republic II.368d-369a). This first city arises because human beings are needy, since the founding premise is that a city is a remedy for human neediness (II.369b-c). Aristotle would later dispute that premise, holding instead that the city is something natural to human beings (Politics I.2, 1252b-1253a). The second argument lays down rules for what may be said about the gods, and in doing so Plato enters a quarrel already about two hundred years old (Republic II.377b-383c). Homer and Hesiod were the nearest thing Greece had to scripture, and their gods lied, lusted, fought their own kin, and handed out good and evil from two jars. Xenophanes, a philosopher of the sixth century BCE, had mocked those portraits. An Athenian jury condemned Socrates in 399 BCE on charges of impiety and corrupting the young. Plato's answer is to make the city's founders theologians before they are lawgivers, deciding what a god must be before deciding what children may hear.
